source.title: Discover-then-Name: Task-Agnostic Concept Bottlenecks via Automated Concept Discovery
source.authors: Sukrut Rao; S. Mahajan; Moritz Böhle; B. Schiele

record.file_problem: none; full paper and appendix are present
record.tranche_reason: Uses sparse autoencoders to discover and name CLIP concepts for building concept bottleneck models. Its evaluations concern concept quality and classification performance, not whether superposition occurs or its geometry.
record.gate_note: The paper reports SAE concept-consistency and naming evaluations, plus a SUNAttributes Jaccard score. These assess the paper's concept-discovery pipeline in vision models, not the claim versions about superposition, LLM representations, or SAE features as complete canonical units. SAE dimensions, sparsity settings, and reconstruction properties described as training setup are not separate outcome rows.
record.test_reason: The study uses sparse autoencoders on CLIP vision encoders as a tool to discover and name concepts for concept bottleneck classifiers. It reports how well its own pipeline works: human consistency and naming ratings, SUNAttributes Jaccard, and classification accuracy. No result bears on toy-model superposition, capacity, or 1-D features. The SAE-vs-neuron interpretability comparison concerns CLIP vision encoders, not the LLMs V4 names. Nothing tests whether SAE features are complete, stable or canonical units (V5).
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that SAEs yield semantically consistent, nameable concepts from CLIP and support performant task-agnostic CBMs, corroborating the promise of SAEs for concept discovery.
record.recipe_differences: Uses an SAE to decompose CLIP vision features, matches decoder dictionary vectors to CLIP text embeddings, and trains concept-bottleneck classifiers. It does not reproduce the toy-network experiments or geometry measurements of Toy Models of Superposition.
record.method_sensitivity: Concept consistency decreases as dictionary-vector alignment with the assigned text embedding decreases; naming granularity and accuracy depend on the vocabulary.

fits_no_version.finding: In CLIP ResNet-50, SAE nodes were rated more semantically consistent than CLIP neurons named by CLIP-Dissect. Consistency fell with lower dictionary-text alignment, and the low-alignment group rated poorly.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In vision-language encoders, SAE latents are more human-interpretable than raw neurons, but a substantial fraction are not consistent concepts.

fits_no_version.finding: Named SAE concepts reached Jaccard 18.3 on SUNAttributes, versus 22.0 for the CLIP retrieval baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE-discovered and named concepts match ground-truth attributes less well than direct CLIP retrieval.

record.problems: The concept user study sampled 24 nodes in total (15 SAE and 9 CLIP-Dissect nodes) and received 22 responses. The main user-study ratings are presented in a figure without numerical values in the text. The paper does not directly test superposition or feature geometry.

untested.parts: No toy networks, no sparsity-dependent transition, no geometry.
No test of capacity pressure as the cause of polysemanticity.
No test of other causes of polysemantic neurons.
Not tested in LLMs. SAE vs neuron interpretability is shown only in CLIP vision encoders, via a small internal user study (24 nodes, 22 responses).
Completeness, stability and canonicity of SAE features are not tested. Low-alignment nodes are reported as often uninterpretable.
No comparison of 1-D directions with multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: If V4 were broadened beyond LLMs to vision models, Fig. 4 would be weak indirect evidence that SAEs recover more interpretable units than neurons. That evidence comes from a small internal survey reported only as a figure. The classification results (Tab. 1, C1–C3) and interventions (Tab. 2) measure the performance of the authors' own CBM method and are correctly left out of the rows.

versions.untested_parts: No toy-network test of overlapping feature directions, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular superposition geometry.
Does not test whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
Evaluates SAE-discovered concepts in CLIP vision encoders, not the version's stated LLM setting or whether LLM features are distributed across neurons.
Does not establish whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units; it reports concept consistency and naming performance.
Does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multi-dimensional features.

rows.stage_stated: pre-trained CLIP feature extractor; SAE trained on CC3M
rows.operation_detail: Compared named SAE concepts with SUNAttributes ground-truth attributes using per-image Jaccard index.
rows.note: The paper reports the SAE result as 18.3 and the CLIP retrieval baseline as 22.0. This measures attribute agreement, not superposition.
rows.check: This row compares the paper's own naming method (18.3) with a CLIP retrieval baseline (22.0) on SUNAttributes. It is a method-performance value, not a measure of any version.
